title: AWS Kiro — Spec-Driven Development in an Agentic IDE

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

Lesson 7-14 covered spec-driven development (SDD) as a *pattern*: write requirements down as a persistent file before you implement, so intent survives context decay and session handoffs — and it named AWS Kiro as one of the real tools formalizing that pattern, alongside GitHub Spec Kit and the informal "Agent OS" convention. This lesson is the hands-on tool profile 7-14 promised: what Kiro actually is, how it forces the requirements-design-tasks workflow rather than merely supporting it, what runs underneath it, and what it costs. By the end you'll have installed Kiro, run one real small feature through its full spec workflow, and reviewed the generated `requirements.md`, `design.md`, and `tasks.md` files the way you'd review any AI-authored artifact — not rubber-stamped just because the process looked rigorous.

## Amazon's Ground-Up Replacement for Q Developer

Kiro is not Amazon Q Developer with new branding — it's a from-scratch agentic IDE, built on Code OSS (the same open-source base as VS Code), that reached general availability internationally on **May 7, 2026**. Amazon has been explicit that Kiro is the successor: Q Developer's standalone IDE plugins and paid subscriptions stopped accepting new signups on **May 15, 2026**, and existing subscriptions reach full end of support on **April 30, 2027** — a 12-month migration window. Q Developer inside the AWS Management Console, AWS documentation search, and the Slack/Teams integrations are unaffected; this retirement is specifically about the standalone developer-tool product.

The migration path isn't uniform across editors. CLI users get backward compatibility and an automatic config copy. VS Code users land in a near-identical Code OSS environment. JetBrains users get a functional path through ACP. But the Q Developer plugins for JetBrains, Eclipse, and Visual Studio are being discontinued outright, with no direct in-IDE replacement — those users have to move to Kiro's own VS Code-based IDE or its CLI. One more forcing function worth knowing about: newer models, including Claude Opus 4.7, are Kiro-only. A Q Developer subscription doesn't carry over or convert — you sign up for Kiro separately.

## Spec-Driven by Force: requirements.md, design.md, tasks.md

Lesson 7-14 described spec-driven development as a discipline you *choose* to apply — write a spec file, then point Claude Code at it. Kiro takes the opposite stance for its **Feature Specs** workflow: it doesn't let you jump straight to code generation. It generates and maintains three structured markdown files as the actual source of truth, with code treated as a build artifact of the spec rather than the primary deliverable:

- **`requirements.md`** — user stories with acceptance criteria written in **EARS notation** (Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax), following a constrained pattern like *"WHEN a user submits a form with invalid data, THE SYSTEM SHALL display validation errors next to the relevant fields."* EARS isn't an AWS invention — it's a formal requirements notation developed in 2009 by engineers at Rolls-Royce to extract airworthiness requirements for jet engine control systems, since adopted by Airbus, NASA, Intel, and Siemens for safety-critical work. Kiro is the first commercial software IDE to make it the default requirements format for ordinary application code rather than aerospace hardware. You can ask Kiro to "Analyze Requirements" before moving on, and it will flag logical inconsistencies, ambiguities, and gaps in what you've written.
- **`design.md`** — a more free-form technical architecture document: data models, sequence diagrams (in Mermaid), API endpoints, and key decisions, capturing how the system will actually work.
- **`tasks.md`** — a checklist where each task includes implementation steps and a comma-separated list of the requirements it maps back to, giving you traceability from a specific line of code to the specific requirement that justified it. Kiro also builds a dependency graph from this file and groups independent tasks into concurrent "waves" it can execute in parallel — a structural efficiency advantage over the iterative prompt-and-accept loop of a purely conversational tool.

Kiro offers two entry points into this: a **Requirements-First** or **Design-First** variant of Feature Specs when you want full control, and a faster **Quick Plan** mode that auto-generates all three artifacts without approval gates for features you already understand well.

## What's Actually Running Underneath

Kiro runs exclusively on models served through **Amazon Bedrock** — as of mid-2026 that includes Claude Opus 4.7 (the flagship for complex agentic work, with a 1M-token context window), Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and several open-weight models. The default **Auto** routing mode picks the model per task rather than making you choose manually: free-tier users get Sonnet-4.5-class quality or better, paid tiers get Opus-4.6-class quality or better. Because it runs on Bedrock, Kiro operations inherit your AWS IAM role rather than requiring a separate API key — a real convenience if your organization is already AWS-native, and real lock-in if it isn't.

Two supporting features round out the picture. **Steering files** — markdown documents in a `.kiro/steering/` directory — persist your team's tech stack, file structure, and coding conventions across sessions, functioning much like Claude Code's `CLAUDE.md` (lesson 7-4) but scoped specifically to steering Kiro's spec generation. **Agent hooks** are event-driven automations — updating test files on save, scanning for secrets before a commit — the same territory as Claude Code's hooks from lesson 7-11, implemented here as a first-class Kiro feature. Kiro also ships native MCP support, so any MCP server you already built in Part 15 connects here too — the same portability story you've now seen repeat across Cline (lesson 9-12), Codex CLI (lesson 9-9), and now Kiro.

## Pricing, as of Mid-2026

Kiro's tiers, by monthly cost and credit allocation: **Free** (50 credits/month, core features), **Pro** at $20/month (1,000 credits), **Pro+** at $40/month (2,000 credits), **Pro Max** at $100/month (5,000 credits, announced at AWS Summit New York on June 17, 2026, aimed squarely at the gap heavy users felt between Pro+ and the $200 Power tier), and **Power** at $200/month (10,000 credits). Overages on every paid tier bill at $0.04 per credit. Kiro is available with a billing address in well over 100 countries, plus AWS GovCloud (US) for regulated workloads — at roughly a 20% price premium over commercial-region pricing.

None of this is a one-time decision. Credits burn differently depending on how much of your work runs through the full Feature Specs workflow versus lighter, ungated prompts, so budget a real trial period before committing a team to a specific tier rather than estimating from a pricing page alone.

## Kiro's Forced Structure vs. Claude Code's Optional One

Lesson 7-14 drew a direct line from Claude Code's Plan Mode (Shift+Tab) to full spec-driven development: Plan Mode makes Claude propose a plan and pause for approval, but the plan is ephemeral — gone once the session compacts or ends. A written spec file promotes that plan to something durable. Kiro's contribution to this same idea is to make the durable version *mandatory* for its primary workflow rather than optional: you don't get to skip straight to code inside Feature Specs the way you can choose to skip writing a `SPEC.md` in Claude Code.

That's a genuine tradeoff, not a strict improvement. Forced structure is exactly right for the "SDD is worth it" cases from lesson 7-14 — multi-session features, work a teammate will pick up cold, anything expensive to get wrong. It's real friction for the "vibe coding is fine" cases from that same lesson — solo exploration, a throwaway script, a task small enough to hold in your head. Kiro's own users report the predictable failure mode of forcing structure everywhere: **specification drift**, where `requirements.md` and `design.md` are generated upfront and don't automatically update as implementation reveals new constraints, producing a distinctly waterfall-shaped slowdown when a team doesn't actively revisit the spec files as understanding changes. Treat Kiro as the right tool when you'd have written a spec in Claude Code anyway and want the workflow enforced and tooled around it — not as a replacement for judging, task by task, whether a spec is worth writing at all.

**Not every team wants EARS notation, and that's a legitimate position.** Kiro's own documentation is upfront that EARS is one valid requirements format, not the only one — behavior-driven development (BDD), plain user stories, and acceptance criteria in prose all work for spec-driven development elsewhere, including the worked example in lesson 7-14. Kiro also has documented episodes of getting stuck in loops, repeating the same wrong fix — AWS has attributed some of these to user error, but it's worth going in with the same "trust but verify" posture lesson 9-8 recommended for Devin's autonomous PRs, not the assumption that a rigorous-looking process guarantees a correct result.

**A forced workflow is still only as good as what you feed it.** Kiro's EARS-notation requirements and traceable `tasks.md` give you an unusually strong paper trail — but a paper trail records what you asked for, not whether what you asked for was right. Review `requirements.md` and `design.md` with the same scrutiny lesson 7-14 asked you to apply to a hand-written spec's acceptance-criteria checklist: read every EARS statement and confirm it says what you actually meant, not just what looks structurally correct.

sections.title: Workshop 1 — Install Kiro and Run One Feature Through the Full Spec Workflow
sections.content:
**Goal:** install Kiro, and run one real small feature all the way through requirements.md, design.md, and tasks.md — reviewing every artifact it produces before accepting the result.

**Step 1 — Download and sign in to Kiro** (kiro.dev). The free tier's 50 monthly credits are enough for this workshop.

**Step 2 — Open or create a small real project** — reuse your `ai-course-projects` folder, or a fresh throwaway project with a handful of real files.

**Step 3 — Start a Feature Spec in Requirements-First mode** for one genuinely small feature — a new CLI flag, a validation rule, a small API endpoint. Let Kiro draft `requirements.md` in EARS notation, then run "Analyze Requirements" and read what it flags before approving.

**Step 4 — Let Kiro generate `design.md`.** Read the data model, sequence diagram, and key decisions it proposes. Push back on anything that doesn't match what you actually want — this is your review checkpoint, not a formality.

**Step 5 — Let Kiro generate `tasks.md` and start execution.** Watch which tasks it groups into the same concurrent wave, and confirm that's consistent with the dependencies you'd expect.

**Step 6 — When implementation finishes, review the diff against `requirements.md` and `tasks.md` line by line** — the same discipline lesson 7-14 applied to a hand-written spec's acceptance criteria, now applied to Kiro's own generated artifacts.

**Outcome:** one real feature built end-to-end through Kiro's mandatory spec workflow, with all three generated files reviewed and either accepted or corrected by you.

sections.question: Lesson 7-14 taught that Claude Code's Plan Mode produces an ephemeral plan, and that promoting it to a persistent spec file is a deliberate choice you make when a task warrants it. How does Kiro's Feature Specs workflow differ from that model?
options: Kiro doesn't support spec-driven development at all — it only does direct code generation, unlike Claude Code

Kiro makes the persistent requirements.md / design.md / tasks.md workflow mandatory for Feature Specs rather than optional, so you can't skip straight to code the way you can choose to skip writing a SPEC.md in Claude Code — a genuine tradeoff, not a strict improvement, since it adds friction on tasks where lesson 7-14 would recommend vibe coding
Kiro's spec files are identical to Claude Code's SPEC.md format and the two tools are functionally interchangeable
Kiro only generates design.md and has no equivalent of requirements.md or tasks.md
sections.explanation: This lesson is explicit that Kiro's contribution to the SDD pattern from 7-14 is making the durable spec version mandatory for its primary workflow, not optional — you don't get to jump straight to code inside Feature Specs. That's genuinely well-suited to the 'SDD is worth it' cases from 7-14 (multi-session work, teammate handoffs, high cost of being wrong) but real friction for the 'vibe coding is fine' cases (solo exploration, throwaway scripts) — it's a tradeoff, not a universal upgrade. Kiro does support spec-driven development (A is wrong), its EARS-based requirements.md format is distinct from a hand-written SPEC.md (C is wrong), and it generates all three files, not just design.md (D is wrong).

sections.title: Workshop 2 — Decide When You'd Actually Reach for Kiro
sections.content:
**Goal:** write a concrete personal rule for when Kiro's forced spec workflow is worth its overhead versus a lighter spec in Claude Code versus plain vibe coding — grounded in lesson 7-14's framework, not a vague intention.

**Step 1 — Revisit lesson 7-14's Workshop 2 rule**, if you wrote one, or think through your own recent AI-coding tasks with fresh eyes.

**Step 2 — For three real tasks you can imagine doing in the next month**, classify each one: plain vibe coding, a lightweight hand-written spec in Claude Code, or Kiro's full mandatory Feature Specs workflow. Write down why for each.

**Step 3 — Be specific about the EARS-notation tradeoff:** for which of your three tasks would forcing every requirement into EARS's constrained syntax actually help catch ambiguity, and for which would it just be paperwork?

**Step 4 — Ask Claude.ai to stress-test your rule:** *"Here's my rule for choosing between vibe coding, a hand-written spec in Claude Code, and AWS Kiro's mandatory Feature Specs workflow: [paste your Step 2-3 answers]. What situation does this rule handle badly?"*

**Step 5 — Save the finished rule** somewhere you'll actually see it again before your next multi-session feature.

**Outcome:** a concrete, written decision rule extending lesson 7-14's SDD-vs-vibe-coding framework to specifically cover when Kiro's forced structure is worth adopting.

sections.question: Kiro's tasks.md gives you full traceability — every task links back to the specific EARS requirement that justified it. According to this lesson, what does that traceability actually guarantee?
options: It guarantees the implementation is bug-free, since every task maps to a documented requirement

It guarantees you can trace which requirement justified a given piece of code, but not that the requirement itself was correct or complete — reviewing requirements.md and design.md for accuracy is still your responsibility, the same scrutiny lesson 7-14 asked you to apply to a hand-written spec's acceptance criteria
It replaces the need to run tests, since the tasks.md checklist functions as a full test suite
It guarantees Kiro will never repeat the same wrong fix in a loop, since traceability prevents specification drift by design
sections.explanation: This lesson's warning callout is explicit: a paper trail records what you asked for, not whether what you asked for was right. Traceability tells you which requirement a task came from — it says nothing about whether that requirement was itself correct, complete, or well-specified, which is exactly why reviewing requirements.md and design.md with real scrutiny remains necessary. The lesson also directly contradicts (A) — Kiro has documented looping episodes despite this traceability — and traceability is a documentation mechanism, not a test suite (C) or a guarantee against specification drift (D), which the lesson names as a real, ongoing risk even with mandatory structure.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 9-13.** You understand Kiro as AWS's ground-up, spec-driven replacement for Amazon Q Developer — its mandatory requirements.md/design.md/tasks.md workflow in EARS notation, what runs underneath it on Amazon Bedrock, its mid-2026 pricing tiers, and how its forced structure compares to the optional spec-driven pattern from lesson 7-14. You've built one real feature through its full workflow and reviewed every generated artifact rather than trusting the process by default. Next: lesson 9-14 turns from writing code to checking it — AI-powered security scanning, and an honest look at what these tools still miss.
